_exec_summary.SummaryText:
General Information
Porex - St. Charles currently uses and stores Toluene Diisocyanate (TDI) in quantities up to 90,000 lbs. Porex orders TDI in an 80% Toluene 2,4-diisocyanate CAS # 584-84-9 / 20% Toluene 2,6-diisocyanate CAS # 91-08-7 ratio from two different vendors. Per 48 CFR 68 § 68.130, TDI has a Threshold Quantity of 10,000 lbs. (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2004). TDI falls under the Toxic Liquid classification per the Roadmap to Offsite Consequence Analysis (OCA) Guidance (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009). 
The site has a North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Code of 326150 and a Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) Code of 3086. 
Basis for Calculations
Porex  St. Charles is subject to 48 CFR 68 based on the following criteria 
	The owner or operator of a stationary source  YES (Porex  St. Charles)
	That has more than a threshold quantity  YES (> 10,000 lbs.)
	Of a regulated substance  YES (TDI)
	In a process.  YES (Storage and Use) (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2004)
With that being said the following information is used to calculate the Distance to a Toxic Endpoint per the Risk Management Program (RMP) Guidance for Offsite Consequence Analysis (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009). Once a determination of Distance to Toxic Endpoint has been made, the determination of which level (I, II, or III) St. Charles is at can be decided. With the level defined Porex can then determine if an alternate release scenario calculation is necessary.
Offsite Consequence Analysis  Worst-Case Scenario
The steps for performing the analysis are specifically given in the guidance document per the list below 
1.	Determine whether each regulated substance is toxic or flammable, as indicated in the rule or Appendices B and C of this guidance. 
2.	For the worst-case analysis, determine the quantity of each substance held in the largest single vessel or pipe.
3.	Collect information about any passive or active (alternative

scenarios only) release mitigation measures that are in place for each substance. 
4.	For toxic substances, determine whether the substance is stored as a gas, as a liquid, as a gas liquefied by refrigeration, or as a gas liquefied under pressure. For alternative scenarios involving a vapor cloud fire, you may also need this information for flammable substances.
5.	For toxic liquids, determine the highest daily maximum temperature of the liquid, based on data for the previous three years, or process temperature, whichever is higher. 
6.	For toxic substances, determine whether the substance behaves as a dense or neutrally buoyant gas or vapor (see Appendix B, Exhibits B-1 and B-2). For alternative scenarios involving a vapor cloud fire, you will also need this information for flammable substances (see Appendix C, Exhibits C-2 and C-3). 
7.	For toxic substances, determine whether the topography (surface roughness) of your site is either urban or rural as these terms are defined by the rule (see 40 CFR 68.22(e)). For alternative scenarios involving a vapor cloud fire, you will also need this information for flammable substances. (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009)
So working through the list we find the following information 
TDI is considered a TOXIC LIQUID per Exhibit B-2 and its use in our particular process. For the worst-case analysis our largest single vessel is capable of holding 50,000 lbs. of TDI. TDI is stored and used as a LIQUID. The highest daily maximum temperature of TDI based on the monthly maximum daily temperature of 96 °F (35.6 °C) (Regional Climate Centers., 2025). Also per Exhibit B-2 and Appendix D, TDI is considered a Buoyant substance for both the worst-case and alternative case scenarios. The only other factor is the topography of the area surrounding Porex  St. Charles. Based on the 40 CFR 68.22(e), Porex is in an URBAN setting. 
(e) Surface roughness. The owner or operator shall use either urban or rural topography, as appropria

te. Urban means that there are many obstacles in the immediate area; obstacles include buildings or trees. Rural means there are no buildings in the immediate area and the terrain is generally flat and unobstructed. (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2004)
Next we follow the Worst-Case Analysis for Toxic Liquids given in Section 1.5.2 of the Guidance (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009). 
Step 1  The worst-case release scenario would happen when the largest capacity TDI tank had a leak at the welded fitting near the outlet of the tank. Because this leak would occur upstream of any valves there would not be an effective means of stopping the release of all of the contents (50,000 lbs.) into the diked area surrounding the TDI tanks. I would not expect this release to be violent enough to cause a rupture in the adjacent tank. 
Step 2  Estimate the release rate. Using 3.2.3 Releases of Toxic Liquids with Passive Mitigation (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009). Compare the maximum area of a pool at a depth of one centimeter to the diked area.
 A=QS×DF=20,000 square feet				(Equation 3-6)
QS = Quantity released in pounds (50,000 lbs.)
DF = Density Factor (0.40 for TDI from Appendix B, Exhibit B-2)
A = Maximum area of pool = 20,000 square feet
Diked Area=11.5 feet×13 feet+22 feet×22 feet=633.5 square feet
Since the diked area is significantly smaller than the pooled area we use the following equation to calculate the release rate.
QR=1.5×LFA×A=0.00570  (lbs.)?min 				(Equation 3-7)
QR = Release rate (pounds / minute)
1.5 = Wind speed factor for the worst-case scenario
LFA = Liquid Factor Ambient (0.000006 from Appendix B, Exhibit B-2)
A = Diked area (633.5 square feet)
Because our process temperature is 35.6 °C (96 °F) we need in use the release rate correction for toxic liquids released at temperatures between 25 °C and 50 °C. After finding the Temperature Correction Factor (TCF) in Appendix B, Exhibit B-4 we plug into the following equation 
?QR?_C=QR×

TCF=0.00570×2.4=0.01368  (lbs.)?min	
(Equation 3-11)
Because our storage and use of TDI is contained in one room inside of a building we also have to apply the correction factor for a release occurring in a building. So the correction factor is 
?QR?_B=0.1×?QR?_C=0.1×0.01368=0.001368  (lbs.)?min					(Equation 3-10)
We also need to determine if there is a potential for the diked area to overflow from a release this size. The volume of the spill is equal to surface area of pooled spill (20,000 square feet) times one centimeter (0.033 feet) or 660 cubic feet. The volume of the diked area is the surface area (633.5 square feet) times the depth of the area (two feet) or 1267 cubic feet. So we would only fill the diked area to a depth of one foot in this worst-case scenario.
Now that we have estimated the release rate and the total quantity spilled, we can calculate the duration of the vapor release from this release. The maximum duration (t) is going to be quantity of release (50,000 lbs.) divided by corrected release rate (0.001368 lbs. / min) or 36,550,000 minutes.
With all of that done we can now go Exhibit B-2 to find the Toxic Endpoint for TDI in the OCA -Guidance (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2009) to figure out the Distance to Toxic Endpoint. 
Just a couple of questions need to be answered to use Exhibit 2 in the OCA guidance. 
	Toxic endpoint of TDI  0.0070 milligrams / Liter
	Determine Bouyant or Dense  TDI is NEUTRALLY BOUYANT
	As described earlier, Porex is in an URBAN area
	Duration of Release > 60 min
The above information was used in Exhibit 2 to use Reference Table #4 to estimate the Distance to Endpoint (mile). We use QRb / Toxic Endpoint (0.001368 / 0.0070 = 0.1954) to cross reference that in the table. 0.1954 falls into the 0  26 category or a Distance to Endpoint of 0.1 miles (528 ft.).
The closest public receptor is Able welding to our North which is only 178 ft. away

So according to the Exhibit 2-1, Porex St. Charles is a Program Level 2

facility (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2004). The nearest public receptor is within the distance to the endpoint for the worst-case release. The process is NOT subject to the OSHA PSM Standard due to our process not being under pressure. Our process does NOT have an NAICS code listed in 40 CFR §68.10 (Title 40: Protection of Environment, 1999). 

Offsite Consequence Analysis  Alternative Release Case Scenario
The steps for performing the analysis are specifically given in the guidance document per the list below 
Step 1: Select alternative release scenario. 
Step 2: Determine release rate. Estimate the release rate and duration of the release of the toxic liquid, based on your scenario and site-specific conditions. 
Step 3: Determine distance to endpoint. Estimate the alternative scenario distance based on the release rate and toxic endpoint (Chapter 8).

Step 1  For the Alternative Case Scenario, Porex assumes that the discharge pressure gauge in the piping system to the reactors breaks off and TDI sprays out due to the transfer pump being turned on and no TDI making it to the reactor so the pump runs until no material left in large tank (50,000 lbs.).
Step 2  Estimate the release rate. Using above calculations but correcting for TDI everywhere in Reactor room not just diked area. Compare the maximum area of a pool at a depth of one centimeter to the Reator room.
 A=QS×DF=20,000 square feet				(Equation 3-6)
QS = Quantity released in pounds (50,000 lbs.)
DF = Density Factor (0.40 for TDI from Appendix B, Exhibit B-2)
A = Maximum area of pool = 20,000 square feet
Reactor room=50 feet×35 feet-100 sq.feet= 1650 square feet
Since the Reactor room is significantly smaller than the pooled area we use the following equation to calculate the release rate.

QR=1.5×LFA×A=0.01485  (lbs.)?min 				(Equation 3-7)
QR = Release rate (pounds / minute)
1.4 = Wind speed factor for the alternate case scenario
LFA = Liquid Factor Ambient (0.000006 from Appendix B, Exhibit B-

2)
A = Reactor room = 1650 square feet

Because our process temperature is 35.6 °C (96 °F) we need to use the release rate correction for toxic liquids released at temperatures between 25 °C and 50 °C.
?QR?_C=QR×TCF=0.01485×2.4=0.03564  (lbs.)?min
(Equation 3-11)
Because our storage and use of TDI is contained in one room inside of a building we also have to apply the correction factor for a release occurring in a building
?QR?_B=0.1×?QR?_C=0.1×0.03564=0.003564  (lbs.)?min					(Equation 3-10)
Now that we have estimated the release rate and the total quantity spilled, we can calculate the duration of the vapor release from this release. The maximum duration (t) is going to be quantity of release (50,000 lbs.) divided by corrected release rate (0.003564 lbs. / min) or 14,029,000 minutes.
Step 3 - Just a couple of questions needed to find the Distance to Endpoint. 
	Toxic endpoint of TDI  0.0070 milligrams / Liter
	Determine Bouyant or Dense  TDI is NEUTRALLY BOUYANT
	As described earlier, Porex is in an URBAN area
	Duration of Release > 60 min
The above information was used in Exhibit 2 to use Reference Table #4 to estimate the Distance to Endpoint (mile). We use QRb / Toxic Endpoint (0.003564 / 0.0070 = 0.5091) to cross reference that in the table. 0.5091 falls into the 0  26 category or a Distance to Endpoint of 0.1 miles (528 ft.).
To estimate the number of people (E_P) within this endpoint the following calculation was used.
E_p=?Pop?_Swan??Area?_Swan ×?Area?_DtE
?Pop?_Swan=Population of Swan Creek Township
?Area?_Swan=23.4 square miles
?Area?_DtE=?r^2=??(DtE)?^2
?Area?_DtE=??(0.1)?^2=0.0314 square miles
E_p=2414?23.4×0.0314 = 4 people
